title: Palindromic Substrings
directAnswer: Count how many contiguous substrings are palindromes (each character is a palindrome of length 1, and longer ones add on). The clean answer reuses Longest Palindromic Substring's engine: expand around each of the 2n−1 centers and add 1 to the count for every successful expansion — O(n²) time, O(1) space. A DP table over dp[i][j] is the same complexity but uses O(n²) space.

remember.pattern: Expand around center — count, don't measure
rules: Every successful expansion is one **more** palindrome — `count++` *inside* the while loop, not after it.
Run **both** center types per index: `(i, i)` for odd lengths and `(i, i+1)` for even lengths — 2n − 1 centers total.
Single characters always count: the loop fires at least once for every `(i, i)` center.
The DP recurrence is `dp[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && (j−i < 2 || dp[i+1][j−1])`; fill by **increasing substring length** or you'll read unfilled cells.
Prefer center-expansion in interviews — same O(n²) time but O(1) space and far less index bookkeeping than the table.
whenToUse: Count (rather than find) substrings with a symmetric, center-growable property
n is modest (≤ ~1000) so O(n²) is fine
You already know expand-around-center from Longest Palindromic Substring
Need both odd and even palindromes tallied in one pass per index
antiSignals: Distinct palindromic substrings only → needs hashing or Eertree, not raw counting
Palindromic subsequences → interval DP, different recurrence
Longest one, not the count → track (start, len) instead of incrementing
n is huge with tight limits → Manacher's gives O(n)
remember.takeaway: Counting palindromic substrings is the same center-expansion trick as finding the longest — you just increment a counter on every successful step instead of comparing lengths. One engine, two problems: see the center and you've solved both.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize this as Longest Palindromic Substring's twin and reuse center expansion — and whether you correctly count every palindrome, including the n trivial single characters.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting only once per center instead of once per successful expansion, or forgetting even-length centers so 'aaa' undercounts.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note out loud that this is the same engine as LC 5, increment inside the expansion loop, and offer the DP table as the alternative while explaining why expansion wins on space.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, return **the number of palindromic substrings** in it.

A **substring** is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string. Two substrings are counted separately if they start or end at different indices, **even if they consist of the same characters**.

Every single character is a palindrome, so the answer is at least `s.length`.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
Substrings at different index ranges count separately even if equal as strings
The answer fits comfortably in a 32-bit integer (max ~500500 for n = 1000)
understanding: Tally every contiguous slice that reads the same both ways. The same letters at a different position count as a separate palindrome — we count index ranges, not distinct strings. 'aaa' has 6: three single chars, two 'aa', and one 'aaa'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do duplicate strings at different positions count separately?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. In 'aaa' the two 'aa' substrings (indices 0–1 and 1–2) are both counted. We count ranges, not distinct strings.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are single characters counted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — each is a palindrome of length 1, so the answer is at least n.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Distinct palindromes or all of them?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: All of them. If they wanted distinct substrings I'd need a hash set or an Eertree; the prompt asks for the raw count.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big does the count get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Worst case is all-equal characters: n(n+1)/2 palindromes. For n = 1000 that's ~500k, well within a 32-bit int.

examples.explanation: Only the three single characters "a", "b", "c" are palindromes.
"a"×3, "aa"×2, "aaa"×1 = 6. Duplicate strings at different indices each count.
"a", "b", "a" (3 singles) plus "aba" = 4. No even-length palindrome here.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both viable approaches are O(n²) time; the deciding factor is space and how much index bookkeeping you want to risk.

approaches.name: Expand Around Center — Count (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. Frame it as 'same engine as Longest Palindromic Substring, but I increment a counter instead of comparing lengths'.
hints: You already know how to find the longest palindrome by growing from a center. What changes if you want the COUNT instead of the longest?
Each time an expansion from a center succeeds (characters match in bounds), you've discovered exactly one more palindrome. Increment then.
Loop every index, expand both the odd center (i, i) and the even center (i, i+1), and add 1 per successful step of each expansion.
approaches.complexityReasoning: 2n−1 centers, each expanding at most O(n) steps with O(1) work per step → O(n²) time. Only an integer counter is stored → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk every index. From each, expand two pointers outward for the odd center `(i, i)` and again for the even center `(i, i+1)`, incrementing a global counter on each successful match. Sum across all centers.

**The reframing from LC 5.** Longest Palindromic Substring asks *how far* each center reaches and keeps the maximum. This problem asks *how many* palindromes exist — and here's the key observation: a center that expands `k` times has discovered exactly `k` palindromes (the length-1 core, then length-3, length-5, … for odd; length-2, length-4, … for even). So instead of comparing lengths after the loop, you `count++` *inside* the loop, once per successful expansion step. Same traversal, different accumulator.

**Why the increment is inside the loop, not after.** A common bug is to expand fully and then add 1 — that counts each center as a single palindrome and throws away all the nested ones. The whole point is that every concentric layer is its own palindrome: in 'aaa', the center at index 1 expands twice ('a' → 'aaa'), contributing 2, not 1. Putting `count++` as the first statement of each successful iteration captures every layer.

**Why both center types, every index.** Odd centers `(i, i)` catch 'a', 'aba', 'ababa'; even centers `(i, i+1)` catch 'aa', 'abba'. Run both at each index and you've covered all 2n − 1 centers. Skipping even centers undercounts any string with repeated adjacent characters — exactly the worst case the problem is built around.
approaches.insight: A center expanding k times = k palindromes, because each concentric ring is itself a palindrome. That's why counting is just 'increment per successful expansion' — you're tallying rings, not centers. Recognizing that nesting structure is what turns the longest-palindrome engine into a counter for free.

dryRun.intro: Increment count on every successful expansion step, across both odd and even centers.

steps.action: 'a' → +1; even (2,3) out of bounds, no add

code.python:
def countSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
    n = len(s)

    def expand(l: int, r: int) -> int:
        found = 0
        while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
            found += 1
            l -= 1
            r += 1
        return found

    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += expand(i, i)
        total += expand(i, i + 1)
    return total

java.explanation: Odd-length palindromes centered on character i.
Even-length palindromes centered on the gap between i and i+1.
Each successful expansion is one more palindrome — increment inside the loop, not after.

pitfalls: Adding 1 after the expansion instead of once per step — counts each center as a single palindrome.
Skipping the even center (i, i+1) — undercounts every repeated-adjacent run.
Using a too-small integer type for huge inputs — though n=1000 maxes at ~500k, fine for int.

approaches.name: DP Table over dp[i][j]
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the alternative if asked to show the DP formulation, or when the interviewer wants the classic table. Note it trades O(n²) space for the same time.
hints: Define dp[i][j] = is the substring s[i..j] a palindrome? How does a longer palindrome relate to a shorter one inside it?
s[i..j] is a palindrome iff its ends match (s[i]==s[j]) AND its interior s[i+1..j-1] is already known to be a palindrome.
Fill the table by increasing substring length (or iterate i downward, j upward) so dp[i+1][j-1] is computed before dp[i][j]. Count every true cell.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Filling an n×n table with O(1) work per cell is O(n²) time; the table itself is O(n²) space.
approaches.explanation:
Let `dp[i][j]` be true when `s[i..j]` is a palindrome. A substring is a palindrome exactly when its two ends match and the strictly-inner substring is also a palindrome. Count every cell that turns out true.

**The recurrence and its base cases.** `dp[i][j] = (s[i] == s[j]) && (j − i < 2 || dp[i+1][j-1])`. The `j − i < 2` guard covers the two base cases with no inner substring: length 1 (`i == j`) is always a palindrome, and length 2 (`j == i+1`) is a palindrome iff the two characters match. For length ≥ 3 the answer leans on the smaller, already-solved `dp[i+1][j-1]`.

**Why fill order matters.** `dp[i][j]` depends on `dp[i+1][j-1]` — a shorter substring sitting one step inside. If you fill in the wrong order you'll read a cell that hasn't been computed yet and get garbage. Two correct orders: iterate by increasing substring length, or run the outer loop `i` from `n−1` down to `0` and the inner `j` from `i` up to `n−1`. Either guarantees the inner cell is ready.

**Why we still prefer expansion in an interview.** This table is conceptually clean and a great way to *show* you understand palindromic DP, but it pays O(n²) memory for the same O(n²) time as center expansion, and the fill-order trap is an easy place to slip. State it as the DP formulation, then point out that expand-around-center gets the identical complexity in O(1) space.
approaches.insight: The table makes the nesting explicit: a palindrome is two matching ends wrapped around a smaller palindrome. That's literally the same concentric-ring idea center expansion exploits — the table just memoizes it instead of recomputing on the fly.

pitfalls: Filling i ascending without the right inner dependency — reads dp[i+1][j-1] before it's set.
Forgetting the j - i < 2 guard so length-2 palindromes try to read a non-existent inner cell.
Allocating O(n²) booleans when O(1)-space center expansion would do — wasteful for large n.

commonMistakes: Incrementing once per center instead of once per successful expansion — undercounts nested palindromes.
Forgetting even-length centers, so strings like "aaa" come up short.
In the DP version, filling the table in an order that reads dp[i+1][j-1] before it's computed.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting once per center, not per layer
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A center that expands k times contains k palindromes. Adding 1 after the loop ignores the nested ones, so 'aaa' returns far less than 6.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping even-length centers
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only expanding (i, i) misses 'aa', 'abba', etc. For repeated-character strings — the worst case — the count is badly low.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong DP fill order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: dp[i][j] needs dp[i+1][j-1]. Iterating i from 0 upward reads that inner cell before it's set, producing wrong counts.
